title: I MAXED OUT my Claude subscription to build this game with Godot
author: fariazz
selftext: Third part of the series where I share how I build a procedural planet game with Claude Code and Godot, in this video the focus is on getting the most of the 5-hour quota.

replies.author: fariazz
replies.body:
I'm glad you liked it :) That video is the third part of the series, this is the first one: [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JPFRmiIN-Oc](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JPFRmiIN-Oc)

The initial prompt was kind of long as it mixed my dictation with a previous conversation I had had with ChatGPT, as explained in the video I also put in some concept images generated by ChatGPT.  
  
 Reddit has a 10k characters and the prompt has \~12k, so I cut the last bit (it was just ChatGPT repeating itself):

\`\`\`  
Create an interactive HTML game design document for this game, make sure to scope it well so it can be done in less than 45 minutes of AI coding. Scope out how many 3D models we'll need in Blender. Any image needed for GUI needs to be created using python/code, same as for all music and sound effects. Context:

Help me brainstorm how I could generate a tiny macro version of a game like No Man's Sky. Essentially, what I would do is firstly use the Blender MCP to create, like, props, like trees and things like that. Let's say different, like, biome elements. Then with Godot, I wanna generate just, like, a Perlin noise procedural terrain where these things are placed, and I guess there's also, like, a randomness or a proceduralness as the type of planet or the biome. And then based on that, all of the assets that are gonna go there are the ones that correspond to that biome, and potentially they could also be, like, tinted, their material be tinted, so that they look different. Like the sky could have a certain color, the earth could have a certain color. So you can wander around in a first-person camera, and then you need to have a spaceship so you can fly over the thing. It needs to have some kind of, I guess, LOD or chunk system so that it's only loading the areas that are near you. And if you go off planet, it's not gonna be, like, a full rounded planet, like a sphere, like in No Man's Sky. You're just gonna get far enough of the land, and then you're, like, in space, and the planet might just be a sphere or something with some kind of shade there, some texture. They all kind of look the same, but using the colors of that planet. So then you can kind of travel to different planets. In terms of mechanics, I'm thinking just really simple, so maybe collecting those red crystals for fuel, so that you can collect fuel to do these trips to fly around, and having some kind of multi-tool to, like, extract elements, like different materials, maybe being able to build. Let's not add something as complex as base building, but maybe you need to build some something, weapons, or something related maybe, like some kind of survival mechanic, I guess. And I think this is totally doable with Blender plus Godot, and I'm pretty inspired, almost thinking of doing a second video today.

…

Yes. The trick is to build the illusion of No Man’s Sky, not the systems that actually make No Man’s Sky work. What you described is very achievable as a small Godot prototype, especially if the goal is a compelling video rather than a durable game.

I’d structure it around one loop:

Land → explore → mine fuel/materials → craft/activate something → launch → choose another planet → repeat.

The planet generator could be surprisingly small. Give each planet a deterministic seed, then derive maybe 6–8 parameters from it: biome archetype, terrain noise settings, ground palette, sky/fog palette, vegetation palette, prop density, crystal/mineral type, and perhaps gravity. The important part is that the combination changes, rather than generating genuinely novel content. Six Blender asset families × palette variation × terrain variation can already produce a lot of apparent diversity.

For example, Blender MCP could generate a reusable asset kit rather than individual planets: 4–5 tree/plant forms, rocks, crystals, weird alien formations, perhaps giant mushrooms, dead trees, and a few "rare" structures. Make everything low-poly and deliberately stylized. Then Godot assigns materials procedurally. One tree mesh could become blue foliage/purple trunk on planet A, orange foliage/black trunk on B, etc. You could even have the generator non-uniformly scale assets so the same plant family produces tiny shrubs on one planet and huge alien trees on another.

I wouldn't actually make spherical planets

Your fake transition idea is much better.

On the surface, you're on an effectively infinite/large planar procedural terrain divided into chunks. Something like a 3×3 or 5×5 chunk grid around the player is enough. Each chunk generates height from FastNoiseLite, then scatters biome props according to noise + seeded RNG.

When the ship reaches, say, 300–500 m altitude:

surface → clouds/fog → fade/transition → space scene.

Unload the terrain entirely. Now the planet is just a sphere with a generated material using the same palette/seed. Put several other spheres in the space scene at exaggeratedly small distances. Flying toward one eventually triggers:

space → atmosphere → fade → generated surface for planet seed N.

That gets you the psychological experience of surface-to-space travel without planetary geometry, floating-origin problems, spherical terrain, planetary gravity, enormous draw distances, etc.

I'd actually exaggerate the transition visually. As you ascend, increase atmospheric haze until visibility approaches zero, then seamlessly switch scenes inside the haze. Coming down does the reverse. It'll look intentional.

The procedural generation can stay tiny

You don't even need sophisticated Perlin composition. Something approximately like:

height = continental\_noise \* 20 + detail\_noise \* 4

Then a second noise map controls vegetation density, another determines rocks/resources, and slope determines whether objects can spawn.

The interesting generator is really the planet descriptor:

PlanetSeed: 48392



Biome: Crystal Forest

Ground: #453c61

Sky: #db795c

Fog: #9b718e



Terrain:

  roughness = 0.35

  mountain\_height = 18



Flora:

  tree\_03

  mushroom\_01

  grass\_02



Resources:

  red\_crystal

  iron\_rock



Temperature: Cold

Hazard: Low

Gravity: 0.82

That descriptor drives everything. It also makes the project very agent-friendly because you can tell the coding agent: given this descriptor, generate the world.

Gameplay: I'd avoid weapons initially

Combat immediately means enemies, AI, animations, health, hit detection, feedback, balancing, etc. That's a huge expansion for relatively little demonstration value.

Instead, make the multitool a mining beam. Point at a red crystal → beam → crystal cracks/disappears → +12 Fuel.

Have perhaps three resources:



Red crystal — Star Fuel: required for interplanetary jumps.

Blue mineral — Energy: recharges multitool/life support.

Metal — Repair material: used for one simple crafting objective.

Then give each planet one discoverable thing. For example, an ancient beacon requiring 20 Metal + 10 Crystal. Activate it and it reveals a new planet or gives a technology upgrade.

That gives you a purpose without building an actual survival game.

You could also introduce a very cheap progression system:

Multitool I → Multitool II → Jetpack → Hyperdrive II

They're basically numbers. Multitool II mines faster; jetpack changes movement; Hyperdrive II allows travel to a previously locked planet. Suddenly there's a game loop.

A particularly good procedural trick

Don't make biome = planet.

Generate two environmental zones per planet using a very low-frequency noise map. Planet A might therefore be "purple forest" overall, but valleys have mushrooms/crystals while highlands have dead trees/rocks.

That will make walking/flying around feel dramatically more procedural without requiring more assets:

planet seed

↓

planet archetype

↓

terrain noise

↓

local biome noise

   ↙      ↘

forest   highlands

And the ship suddenly becomes useful even before going to space: you can fly 30 seconds across the terrain and visibly see the environment change.

Scope I'd use for the video

I'd aim for 3 planet archetypes, \~15 Blender assets, one ship, one multitool, three resources, one craftable/activatable technology, chunked procedural terrain and fake seamless surface↔space transitions.

Planet 1: lush/weird forest.

Planet 2: red barren desert with huge rocks/crystals.

Planet 3: bizarre fluorescent mushroom/crystal world.

The underlying code can be almost identical for all three.

And this fits the Blender MCP → Godot story unusually well because Blender isn't decorative here. The video has a very clean progression: prompt generates an alien asset library → agent builds procedural world generator → suddenly those assets form effectively unlimited planets → add spaceship → leave the planet → another generated world appears.

The reveal at the end can be much bigger than the actual technical scope. You start the video with a handful of disconnected Blender props and finish flying from one generated alien world to another.

I would not add base building, inventory grids, NPCs, procedural creatures, combat, spherical terrain, orbital mechanics, or realistic solar-system scale. Those are precisely the things that turn this from a one-day/two-day agentic build into a game project.

Generate a few different screenshots of what the game will look like. So give me maybe two to three in planet and then give me one of when you're in space. I guess when you're in space, I'm not sure if we're going to see the spaceship as a third-person character or if it's a first-person as well, but you have the cabin. So that needs to be defined.
